title: 2026 Usage Policy update
gist: Anthropic's 2026 Usage Policy update (effective Nov 12) mostly clarifies rules for more autonomous Claude use: a consolidated ban on deceptive/influence campaigns, narrower election rules that drop the blanket ban on personalized vote targeting, explicit bans on weapon guidance software and surveillance tooling, human-in-the-loop and fail-safe requirements for high-risk and physical-hardware uses, a new prohibition on extreme abuse of models, and ownership-based Supported Regions enforcement.

themes.theme: Policy cadence tied to agentic capability

insights.claim: Anthropic's 2026 Usage Policy update is mostly clarification of existing rules, driven by Claude taking on longer, more independent (agentic) work over the past year.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Governance surface expands with model autonomy; expect usage-policy scope to keep growing as agentic deployments scale.
insights.quote: In the year since our last refresh, Claude has taken on longer, more independent work.
insights.locator: Each year, Anthropic updates its Usage Policy

insights.claim: The updated Anthropic Usage Policy takes effect on November 12, 2026, and draws on misuse patterns observed over the past year in influence operations, weapons development and surveillance.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Enterprise and API customers have a compliance deadline; misuse telemetry from threat intel reports directly feeds policy.
insights.quote: The updated policy takes effect on November 12.

insights.claim: Anthropic commits to keep revising its Usage Policy as Claude's capabilities and risks change, with input from policymakers, experts, civil society and users.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Policy is a moving target; platforms building on Claude should budget for recurring compliance review.

insights.claim: State media outlets, government propaganda offices and commercial firms have used Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Frontier LLMs are actively being used as infrastructure for influence ops, both state and commercial, raising regulatory and reputational exposure for AI providers.
insights.quote: we’ve seen examples of state media outlets, government propaganda offices, and commercial firms using Claude to run networks of fake accounts and fabricated news sites
insights.locator: A new section on deceptive activity

insights.claim: Anthropic consolidated scattered election, fraud, privacy and disinformation rules into one section, 'Do Not Engage in Deceptive Campaigns or Artificial Activity', covering political and commercial deception including building influence-operation tooling.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Commercial astroturfing (fake reviews, bot amplification vendors) is now explicitly in scope alongside political ops.
insights.quote: which applies to deceptive activity of any kind (whether political or commercial)

insights.claim: Anthropic removed its blanket ban on personalized vote and campaign targeting because it blocked legitimate civic work, narrowing election rules to deceiving voters or disrupting elections.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: A rare loosening: political campaigns, nonprofits and election officials gain a permitted use case for Claude, opening a civic-tech/political-services market segment.
insights.quote: we’ve also removed our blanket prohibition on personalized vote and campaign targeting

insights.claim: People have attempted to use Anthropic's models to build guidance and control software for weapons; the policy now explicitly bans weapon software/components and arming drones and other autonomous vehicles.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Defense-tech firms building autonomy or targeting stacks cannot rely on Claude, pushing that demand toward other model providers or in-house models.
insights.quote: Recently, we’ve seen people attempt to use our models to build guidance and control software for weapons.

insights.claim: Anthropic's September threat intelligence report documented growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: AI-enabled repression is an observed, rising misuse vector, likely to shape export-control and regional-access policy.
insights.quote: documented the growing use of AI to build surveillance systems that identify and track political dissidents

insights.claim: Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest or charge, nor to build or improve surveillance tools, while consented tracking (e.g. fraud monitoring), content moderation, journalism and legal research remain permitted.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Predictive-policing and surveillance vendors are excluded as customers; fraud/compliance and trust-and-safety use cases are explicitly safe.
insights.quote: Claude cannot be used to decide or recommend who to investigate, arrest, or charge in a law enforcement or criminal justice process.

insights.claim: Anthropic states the weapons and surveillance rewrites do not change what it enforces in practice; they only make existing enforcement explicit.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: No change in addressable market from these sections; the update reduces ambiguity rather than restricting new customers.
insights.quote: this update does not reflect a change in what we enforce in practice

themes.theme: High-risk use cases and physical autonomy

insights.claim: Uses affecting health, legal rights, finances, livelihood or access to essential services require a qualified human in the loop with authority to change Claude's recommendations, plus disclosure to the affected person that AI was used.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Fully automated AI decisioning in lending, insurance, healthcare and HR on Claude is not permitted; deployment economics in these verticals must include human reviewers.
insights.quote: we require there to be a qualified “human in the loop”
insights.locator: Clearer requirements for high-risk use cases

insights.claim: Following its Model Hardware Standard, Anthropic now requires that when Claude drives hardware capable of injury, a qualified operator can observe and stop it, and the equipment holds a safe state if Claude disconnects.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Signals Claude is being deployed in robotics/physical actuation; robotics integrators face fail-safe and teleoperation design requirements.
insights.quote: the equipment must also be able to hold a safe state if Claude is disconnected
insights.locator: Following the launch of our Model Hardware Standard

insights.claim: Anthropic added a prohibition on sustained, needless abusive or cruel behavior toward its models, limited to extreme repeated cases and excluding frustration, pushback, dark creative themes and model testing.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Model-welfare considerations are moving from research into formal terms of service, a differentiating stance among AI labs.
insights.quote: We’ve added a prohibition on sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.
insights.locator: Addressing abusive behavior toward our models

insights.claim: Claude's ability to end conversations with persistently abusive users on Claude.ai and Claude Code remains the primary enforcement mechanism for the abuse rule.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Enforcement is product-level (conversation termination) rather than account bans, limiting customer friction.
insights.quote: Claude’s ability to end these interactions will remain the primary enforcement mechanism
insights.locator: This addition aligns with a step

insights.claim: Anthropic's Supported Regions Policy bars use by people physically located in unsupported regions, entities incorporated or headquartered there, and entities majority-owned or controlled by persons or entities from those regions.
insights.speaker: @AnthropicAI
insights.so_what: Ownership-based restrictions cut off subsidiaries of firms from unsupported regions (e.g. offshore affiliates), shaping competitive access to frontier models along geopolitical lines.
insights.quote: entities who are majority-owned or controlled by persons or entities in those regions
